1 Samuel 1.audience: The first Israelites who heard this book knew Shiloh as the sanctuary later destroyed and remembered as a warning (Jeremiah 7:12), and they knew Samuel as the prophet who anointed their first kings. They heard that his life began in answer to a woman's prayer.

culture.title: Yearly pilgrimage
culture.text: Elkanah's family went up to Shiloh every year to worship and sacrifice. The sacrifice was followed by a family meal, with portions given to each member (1 Samuel 1:4–5).

culture.title: Two wives
culture.text: A man sometimes took a second wife when the first had no children. Rivalry between wives, as between Hannah and Peninnah, appears also with Sarah and Hagar and with Rachel and Leah.

culture.title: Silent prayer
culture.text: Prayer was normally spoken aloud. Hannah prays silently, moving only her lips, which is why Eli thinks she is drunk.

1 Samuel 2.audience: Israel's priests traced their line through Aaron. Readers would see Eli's house, descended from Aaron, condemned here, and a "faithful priest" promised in its place (1 Samuel 2:35).

culture.title: The priest's fleshhook
culture.text: Peace offerings were boiled in pots for the worshippers' meal. Eli's sons sent a servant with a three-pronged fork to take whatever it brought up, and even demanded raw meat before the fat was burned (1 Samuel 2:15–16), contrary to the law (Leviticus 7:31–34).

culture.title: A linen ephod
culture.text: The young Samuel wore a linen ephod, a simple priestly garment. His mother brought him a little coat each year when the family came to sacrifice (1 Samuel 2:19).

culture.title: Women at the tabernacle door
culture.text: Women served at the entrance of the tabernacle, as also mentioned in Exodus 38:8.

1 Samuel 3.audience: Israel's readers knew Samuel as both the last of the judges and a prophet who anointed Israel's first two kings. This chapter records his call while still a boy serving at Shiloh.

culture.title: Sleeping in the sanctuary
culture.text: Samuel slept in the temple of the LORD, where the ark was, before the lamp of God went out. The lamp burned through the night and was tended at evening and morning (Exodus 27:20–21).

culture.title: Rare visions
culture.text: "The word of the LORD was precious in those days; there was no open vision." The KJV's "precious" here means rare.

culture.title: Dan to Beersheba
culture.text: "From Dan even to Beersheba" was the standard phrase for the whole land, from the northernmost town to the southernmost.

1 Samuel 4.audience: The Philistines were Israel's main enemy in this period. Readers knew that the loss of the ark here was remembered in Israel's worship (Psalm 78:60–61).

culture.title: Taking gods into battle
culture.text: Ancient armies carried images or symbols of their gods into battle for victory. Israel brings the ark from Shiloh in the same way, and the Philistines react as though Israel's gods had arrived (1 Samuel 4:7–8).

culture.title: A runner from the battle
culture.text: News of battles was carried by runners. Torn clothes and earth on the head were signs of grief and bad news.

culture.title: Ichabod
culture.text: Phinehas's wife names her son Ichabod, explained as "The glory is departed from Israel." Names were often chosen to mark the circumstances of a birth.

1 Samuel 5.audience: The first Israelites who heard this book knew the Philistines as worshipers of Dagon (Judges 16:23) and as the people who held the ark for seven months. They heard that the LORD showed his power inside the Philistines' own temple.

culture.title: Captured gods in temples
culture.text: Victors often carried the images of defeated peoples' gods to their own temples as trophies, placing them before their own god. The Philistines put the ark beside Dagon.

culture.title: The threshold of Dagon
culture.text: The text notes that Dagon's priests still did not step on the threshold of his temple in Ashdod "unto this day."

1 Samuel 6.audience: The first Israelites who heard this book knew Bethshemesh as a town given to the priests (Joshua 21:16) and knew the law that the holy things must not be looked on (Numbers 4:20). They heard how the ark came home with joy and then with fear.

culture.title: Guilt offering of gold
culture.text: Philistine priests and diviners advise sending five golden emerods (tumors) and five golden mice, one for each Philistine lord, as a trespass offering—images of the plague returned to the god who sent it.

culture.title: Milk cows and their calves
culture.text: Cows that had never been yoked, with calves shut up at home, would naturally turn back toward their young. Going straight toward Bethshemesh was taken as a sign.

1 Samuel 7.audience: The first Israelites who heard this book remembered the shame of the lost ark and the long years of Philistine pressure. They heard that Israel's turn back to the LORD, not the ark, brought rescue, and that the stone Ebenezer was set up as a reminder.

culture.title: Pouring out water
culture.text: At Mizpeh the people draw water and pour it out before the LORD, fast, and confess their sin. The water rite is not described elsewhere in the law.

culture.title: Ebenezer
culture.text: Samuel sets up a stone and names it Ebenezer, which means stone of help. Standing stones commonly marked places of victory or covenant.

1 Samuel 8.audience: Readers lived under kings and knew the burdens Samuel lists—conscription, forced labor, taxes, and land taken for royal servants (1 Samuel 8:11–17). After Solomon's reign the people complained that he had made their yoke grievous (1 Kings 12:4).

culture.title: Kings of the nations
culture.text: All of Israel's neighbors had kings. Ancient Near Eastern kings led armies, kept courts and chariot forces, and collected taxes.

culture.title: A tenth for the king
culture.text: The king would take a tenth of grain, vineyards, and flocks—a tax in addition to the tithe given to the LORD.

1 Samuel 9.audience: Saul's tribe, Benjamin, was the smallest in Israel (1 Samuel 9:21). Readers would note that Israel's first king came from a minor family of a small tribe.

culture.title: Seer and prophet
culture.text: The text explains that a prophet was formerly called a seer, a note written for later readers when the older term had fallen out of use.

culture.title: A gift for the man of God
culture.text: People bringing a question to a seer brought a gift. Saul's servant offers a quarter of a shekel of silver.

culture.title: Feast at the high place
culture.text: Before the temple was built, sacrifices were offered at local high places, followed by a shared meal. Samuel seats Saul in the chief place and gives him the reserved shoulder.

1 Samuel 10.audience: The first Israelites who heard this book knew Gibeah as Saul's royal town and knew that Saul's reign ended badly. They heard how he was chosen with signs and a public lot, and that some people doubted him from the start.

culture.title: Anointing with oil
culture.text: Samuel pours oil on Saul's head. Anointing set a person apart for office; kings were called "the LORD's anointed." The Hebrew word for anointed one is the source of "Messiah."

culture.title: Bands of prophets
culture.text: Groups of prophets traveled together with harps, tambourines, pipes, and lyres. Similar companies, called "sons of the prophets," appear in the days of Elijah and Elisha (2 Kings 2:3).

culture.title: Choosing by lot
culture.text: Saul is chosen publicly by lot, narrowing from tribe to family to person. The same method identified Achan (Joshua 7:16–18).

1 Samuel 11.audience: The first Israelites who heard this book knew that the men of Jabeshgilead later rescued and buried Saul's body (1 Samuel 31:11–13), repaying this rescue. They heard Saul act as a deliverer, like the judges before him, and show mercy after the victory.

culture.title: Gouging out right eyes
culture.text: Nahash demands the right eye of every man as a reproach on all Israel. The Jewish historian Josephus explained that it would leave them unfit for battle, since a shield held in the left hand covered the left eye.

culture.title: A summons with pieces
culture.text: Saul cuts a yoke of oxen in pieces and sends them through Israel, threatening the same to the oxen of anyone who does not come. A similar summons was sent in Judges 19:29.

1 Samuel 12.audience: The first Israelites who heard this book had lived under kings and knew how many of them led the people away from the LORD. They heard Samuel's farewell as a warning that both king and people must obey the LORD.

culture.title: Thunder at wheat harvest
culture.text: Wheat harvest came in early summer, the dry season, when rain almost never falls in Israel. Thunder and rain then were an unmistakable sign.

culture.title: A public accounting
culture.text: Samuel asks whether he has taken anyone's ox or donkey, defrauded or oppressed anyone, or taken a bribe. A leader stepping down could ask the people to testify to his honesty.

1 Samuel 13.audience: The first Israelites who heard this book knew the weight of Philistine rule, and they knew that Samuel had told Saul to wait seven days for him (1 Samuel 10:8). They heard that Saul's first big failure came when he took the priest's work into his own hands.

culture.title: No smiths in Israel
culture.text: The Philistines controlled metalworking, so Israelites had to go to them to sharpen farm tools. The pim, a weight of about two-thirds of a shekel, was the charge (in the KJV, "a file").

culture.title: Hiding in caves
culture.text: The limestone hills of Israel are full of caves, rock clefts, and cisterns, which served as hiding places in times of invasion.

1 Samuel 14.audience: The first Israelites who heard this book knew that their army had few weapons (1 Samuel 13:19–22). They heard that Jonathan's attack with only his armourbearer was all the more striking, and that a king's rash oath could hurt his own people.

culture.title: Armourbearer
culture.text: A warrior's armourbearer carried his shield and extra weapons and finished off enemies he struck down (1 Samuel 14:13).

culture.title: Eating with the blood
culture.text: Exhausted soldiers slaughter animals on the ground and eat meat with the blood, breaking the law of Leviticus 17:10–14. Saul has a large stone brought so the animals can be properly slaughtered.

culture.title: Seeking an answer
culture.text: Lots were cast to find who had broken Saul's oath. The Greek translation of this verse mentions Urim and Thummim.

1 Samuel 15.audience: The Amalekites had attacked Israel in the wilderness (Exodus 17:8–16; Deuteronomy 25:17–19). Readers knew this chapter as the reason Saul lost the kingdom.

culture.title: Devoted to destruction
culture.text: The command to "utterly destroy" meant devoting everything to the LORD, with no plunder kept. Saul spares King Agag and the best animals.

culture.title: A victory monument
culture.text: Saul sets up a monument ("a place") at Carmel in Judah. Kings commonly erected victory monuments.

culture.title: Grasping a robe
culture.text: Saul seizes the hem of Samuel's robe and it tears. Samuel uses it as a sign: "The LORD hath rent the kingdom of Israel from thee this day."

1 Samuel 16.audience: The first Israelites who heard this book knew Jesse's family from the end of Ruth (Ruth 4:17–22) and knew David as their greatest king. They heard that God chose him while he was still a shepherd and the youngest of his brothers.

culture.title: Youngest son as shepherd
culture.text: Tending sheep was often given to the youngest son or daughter. David is out with the flock while his older brothers are presented.

culture.title: Music for distress
culture.text: Music was used to soothe troubled minds. David plays the harp (lyre) for Saul when the evil spirit comes upon him.

1 Samuel 17.audience: The first Israelites who heard this book knew the Philistines as their long-time enemy and knew David's victory over Goliath as the start of his rise. Goliath's sword was later kept at Nob (1 Samuel 21:9). They heard that David won by trusting the LORD, not weapons.

culture.title: Single combat
culture.text: Ancient armies sometimes settled battles by a contest between champions. Goliath proposes that the loser's people serve the winner's.

culture.title: Goliath's armor
culture.text: Goliath wears a bronze helmet, scale armor weighing 5,000 shekels (about 125 pounds), bronze greaves, and carries a javelin and a spear with an iron head of 600 shekels.

culture.title: The sling
culture.text: Shepherds used slings to protect their flocks. A skilled slinger could hurl a smooth stone with great speed and accuracy; slingers were a regular part of ancient armies (Judges 20:16).

1 Samuel 18.audience: Readers knew Jonathan as Saul's heir. His friendship with David, and his gift of his own robe and weapons, is told here (1 Samuel 18:3–4).

culture.title: Victory songs
culture.text: Women came out with tabrets and instruments to greet returning warriors. Their song, "Saul hath slain his thousands, and David his ten thousands," was later known even among the Philistines (1 Samuel 21:11).

culture.title: A bride-price
culture.text: Saul asks no dowry (bride-price) but a hundred Philistine foreskins, hoping David will be killed. A groom normally paid the bride's father.

1 Samuel 19.audience: The first Israelites who heard this book knew Saul's later hatred of David and knew that prophets traveled in groups (1 Samuel 10:5). They heard that even Saul was overcome by prophesying in Samuel's presence, and that Jonathan, Michal, and Samuel all helped David.

culture.title: Escape through a window
culture.text: Michal lets David down through a window, as Rahab did for the spies (Joshua 2:15).

culture.title: An image in the bed
culture.text: Michal puts an image (teraphim, a household idol) in the bed with goats' hair at its head to look like David sleeping.

1 Samuel 20.audience: Readers knew of David's later kindness to Jonathan's son Mephibosheth (2 Samuel 9). This chapter records the covenant between David and Jonathan that lies behind it.

culture.title: The new moon feast
culture.text: The new moon began each month and was marked by sacrifices and a family meal. David's absence from the king's table would be noticed.

culture.title: Arrows as a signal
culture.text: Jonathan uses arrows shot beyond a boy as a pre-arranged signal, so he can warn David without being seen talking to him.

1 Samuel 21.audience: The first Israelites who heard this book knew David as their great king, and they knew that Jesus later pointed to David's eating the holy bread (Mark 2:25–26). They heard that David, God's chosen king, was hungry and afraid, and that he did not tell the truth.

culture.title: The showbread
culture.text: The twelve loaves on the table before the LORD were replaced every Sabbath, and the old loaves were eaten by the priests only (Leviticus 24:5–9).

culture.title: Feigning madness
culture.text: David pretends to be insane before Achish of Gath, scribbling on the gate doors and letting spittle run down his beard. The title of Psalm 34 refers to this occasion.

1 Samuel 22.audience: Readers knew Abiathar, the one priest who escaped Saul's massacre at Nob, as David's priest throughout his reign (1 Kings 2:26–27).

culture.title: The cave of Adullam
culture.text: Adullam was in the lowlands of Judah. Debtors, the discontented, and others in distress gathered to David there, about four hundred men.

culture.title: Family to Moab
culture.text: David leaves his parents with the king of Moab. Through Ruth, David's family had Moabite ancestry (Ruth 4:17).

1 Samuel 23.audience: The first Israelites who heard this book knew these as Judah's own towns, and they heard that some of Judah's people gave David away to Saul (1 Samuel 23:12, 19). They heard that David asked the LORD before he acted and that Jonathan encouraged him.

culture.title: Threshing floors raided
culture.text: Raiders struck at harvest, robbing threshing floors where the year's grain lay in the open.

culture.title: Asking through the ephod
culture.text: Abiathar brings the ephod, and David asks the LORD yes-or-no questions about whether Saul will come and whether the people of Keilah will hand him over.

1 Samuel 24.audience: The first Israelites who heard this book knew that David later became king and that Saul's family fell. They heard that David honored Saul as the king the LORD had anointed, even when he could have killed him, and that Saul admitted David would reign.

culture.title: Covering the feet
culture.text: "To cover his feet" is a polite expression for relieving oneself. Saul enters the very cave where David's men are hiding.

culture.title: The LORD's anointed
culture.text: David refuses to harm Saul because he is "the LORD's anointed." A king's anointing set him apart under God's protection.

culture.title: Cutting the robe
culture.text: David cuts off the corner of Saul's robe. The hem of a garment could represent its owner's status and authority.

1 Samuel 25.audience: The first Israelites who heard this book knew Abigail as one of David's wives and the mother of his son Chileab (2 Samuel 3:3). They heard how her good sense kept David from shedding blood, and that Samuel's death is told in one verse.

culture.title: Sheep-shearing
culture.text: Shearing season was a time of celebration and plenty for flock owners. David's men had protected Nabal's shepherds and expected a gift in return.

culture.title: Gifts to prevent violence
culture.text: Abigail brings bread, wine, dressed sheep, parched grain, raisins, and figs on donkeys—a generous gift to turn away David's anger, as Jacob sent ahead to Esau (Genesis 32:13–20).

1 Samuel 26.audience: Readers knew Abishai and Joab, sons of Zeruiah, as David's fierce commanders. Abishai offers to kill Saul in this chapter.

culture.title: The camp by night
culture.text: Saul sleeps inside a ring of baggage and men, with his spear stuck in the ground at his head—a sign of the king's place in camp.

culture.title: Calling across the valley
culture.text: David crosses to the top of a hill at a distance and calls out. In hill country, voices carry across valleys.

1 Samuel 27.audience: The first Israelites who heard this book knew that Ziklag later belonged "unto the kings of Judah unto this day" (1 Samuel 27:6), and that David's time among the Philistines came before his reign. They heard that fear led David to hard choices.

culture.title: A vassal of Gath
culture.text: Achish gives David a town in exchange for service, a common arrangement between a king and a band of warriors. David lives among the Philistines for a year and four months.

culture.title: Raids in the south
culture.text: David raids the Geshurites, Gezrites, and Amalekites, but tells Achish he has raided southern Judah.

1 Samuel 28.audience: Saul had earlier banned mediums and wizards from the land, as the law required (Leviticus 19:31). Readers would see him break his own ban at Endor.

culture.title: Ways of seeking God
culture.text: Israelites sought guidance through dreams, the Urim, and prophets. Saul receives no answer by any of them.

culture.title: Consulting the dead
culture.text: Necromancy—calling up the spirits of the dead for information—was widespread in the ancient Near East. The woman of Endor is described as having "a familiar spirit."

1 Samuel 29.audience: The first Israelites who heard this book knew that David would soon be king and may have wondered how he escaped fighting his own people. They heard that the Philistine lords themselves sent him away.

culture.title: Mustering by hundreds and thousands
culture.text: The Philistine lords marched past by hundreds and thousands, in units under their commanders.

culture.title: Distrust of a foreign warrior
culture.text: The Philistine commanders fear David might turn on them in battle to win back Saul's favor.

1 Samuel 30.audience: David shares the spoil with the elders of many towns in Judah (1 Samuel 30:26–31). Readers would recognize these as places that later supported him as king in Hebron.

culture.title: Raiders on camels
culture.text: The Amalekites were desert raiders. Four hundred young men escape on camels, which could outrun pursuers on foot.

culture.title: Shares for those who stayed
culture.text: David rules that those who guarded the baggage share equally with those who fought. The text says it became a statute in Israel "unto this day."

1 Samuel 31.audience: The first Israelites who heard this book knew David's lament for Saul and Jonathan (2 Samuel 1:17–27) and remembered how Jabeshgilead honored Saul. They heard how the first king's reign ended in defeat.

culture.title: Displaying the bodies
culture.text: The Philistines cut off Saul's head, sent news to their temples, put his armor in the house of Ashtaroth, and fastened his body to the wall of Bethshan—common ways of celebrating victory.

culture.title: Burning and burial
culture.text: The men of Jabesh burn the bodies and bury the bones under a tree, then fast seven days. Burning the dead was unusual in Israel.
